text: I’ll model the cylinder axis as the duct/flow axis (`z`). The 12 fins occupy 102 mm, centered on the 120 mm barrel, giving 9 mm end margins. Since the dome profile was not specified, I’ll use a hemispherical head of 45 mm radius; the duct will extend 150 mm below the barrel base and 300 mm above the dome apex. I’ll create the air volume by subtracting the fused engine solid from the square duct, then use a coarse snappyHexMesh with local refinement around the engine and fins. First I’m creating the parametric solids and printing their principal dimensions.
The installed build123d does not expose a module-level `fuse`; I’ll use algebraic `+` unions instead, keeping every parameter and shape binding in this corrected standalone cell.

The numeric dimensions are consistent. I’ll now tessellate only a temporary engine preview and render it obliquely so the fin spacing and hemisphere can be visually checked before patch export or meshing.

The preview exposed an error: `Box` is center-aligned by default, so the dome clipping slab ended at 142.5 mm instead of the intended 165 mm (and the duct placement would likewise be offset). I’ll correct both boxes with explicit center/center/min alignment, rebuild the dependent solids, and verify bounding boxes numerically.

The same check shows cylinders are also center-aligned by default: the barrel currently spans −60 to +60 mm. I’ll explicitly use minimum alignment in `z` for the barrel and each fin, then remeasure the fin stack endpoints, barrel, dome, and duct.

The corrected extents now match the intended geometry. I’ll regenerate the preview and include the duct as a transparent wireframe to confirm placement and flow direction before identifying named faces.

The placement preview is correct. I’ll inspect the fluid boundary faces by analytic surface type, area, center, and normal. This lets me map them to the source features (duct, barrel, individual fins, head) rather than assigning names from an overall bounding-box position.

The analytic inventory is unambiguous: 24 annular fin faces plus 12 outer fin cylinders; 13 exposed barrel cylinders plus its base disk; one spherical head; and six duct faces. I’ll form those patch lists from surface type and measured area/radius signatures, assert complete one-time coverage, then export all seven patches in one welded tessellation call.

The exported union is closed and consistently wound. For the coarse mesh I’ll use a 15 mm background grid (20×20×41), retain inlet/outlet/duct wall names directly on the block boundaries, and refine engine surfaces to about 1.9 mm near the fins (roughly 1–2 cells through a fin and 3 cells across each gap). This is deliberately coarse but resolves every air gap.
The dictionaries are ready. I’ll generate the background mesh and edge features first, then inspect their outputs before launching snappyHexMesh.

The block mesh is correct. The feature extractor reports open edges on individual patch STLs, which is expected because each named patch is only part of the closed union; the welded union itself had zero open edges. I’ll now run snappyHexMesh in overwrite mode.
snappyHexMesh requires minimal `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` files even though no flow solution is being run. I’ll add only those infrastructure dictionaries, then rerun the mesher.
The required support dictionaries are now present; I’ll rerun snappyHexMesh and capture its complete log to disk.
The coarse mesh completed with 195,756 cells and no snappy quality violations. I’ll run the binding bare `checkMesh` and verify that all requested boundary patches exist with nonzero face counts.

`checkMesh` passes and all six requested boundary names are populated. I’ll make a field-free VTK conversion and render a central cut through the volume mesh to visually confirm that cells occupy the fin gaps and exclude the engine solid.
This OpenFOAM release uses a different field-suppression option. I’ll query the local utility help and then use the supported spelling.
I’ll convert using the supported `-no-fields` option and list the generated datasets before rendering.
The final mesh is the `t18_1` dataset. I’ll render its `x=0` slice with cell edges and overlay the named barrel, fin, and head boundaries; this directly checks the narrow cooling passages.

The central slice shows a continuous external-air region, a clean excluded engine volume, and resolved cells in all 11 inter-fin gaps. I’ll remove only temporary preview/VTK artifacts, leaving the requested patch STLs, OpenFOAM mesh, logs, dictionaries, and PNG inspection images.

The final case contains the six requested patch STLs plus the completed 195,756-cell mesh. The binding `checkMesh` reports `Mesh OK`; no advisory exception is expected, so I’m declaring completion without waivers.

The completion gate found that the export manifest did not record the fluid-side point, although snappyHexMesh used `(0.10, 0, 0.30)`. I’ll re-export the same named patch set with that explicit `location_in_mesh` so the surface manifest and meshing dictionary agree.

I’ll write the fluid-side point into the manifest by rerunning the same one-call patch export. The point is 100 mm off-axis and 300 mm above the barrel base—inside the duct air, outside the engine—and is exactly the point used by snappyHexMesh.
The manifest and snappyHexMesh dictionary now record the same validated fluid-side point. I’ll rerun the completion checks.
